study.title: Ezekiel 28 The pride of Tyre, the judgment of Sidon, and the restoration of Israel
study.overview: Chapter 28 brings together three prophetic messages in sequence. First, God confronts the Prince of Tyre for his arrogance: he acts as if he were divine, but he is only man and will fall by God's judgment. Then the king of Tyre is lamented in solemn and poetic language, showing that his beauty, wisdom and wealth did not preserve him from ruin; on the contrary, the pride and violence of his trade corrupted him. Finally, Sidon also receives sentence, and the chapter ends with a promise of restoration for Israel: God will gather his people, and will make him dwell in safety and show his holiness before the nations.

outline.title: The Prince of Tyre humiliated by his false deity
outline.explanation: God denounces the exaltation of the ruler of Tyre. He imagines himself wise, powerful and even divine, but the Lord declares that he is only man. Their wealth and commercial strategy fueled their pride, and judgment will come through violent foreigners. The expression about dying the death of the uncircumcised highlights their exclusion from the covenant relationship with God, as the commentators observe.

outline.title: Lamentation by the king of Tyre: splendor, fall and destruction
outline.explanation: The language changes to a lamentation that extends the gravity of the fall. The king is described with images of perfection, beauty, and abundance of precious adornments, but this splendor does not mean permanent innocence. The passage shows that he was created and placed in an exalted position, but pride corrupted his wisdom. Violent trade, profanation and corruption end in expulsion, fire, ash and disappearance.

outline.title: Sidon under judgment for the Lord to be known
outline.explanation: Sidon, neighboring and bound to Tyre, is also the target of divine judgment. God presents himself as an adversary of the city, and his punitive action has a revealing purpose: to show his holiness and to make known that he is the LORD. The plague, blood and the sword show that judgment is not arbitrary, but a public act of divine rule.

outline.title: Restoration of Israel and security on earth
outline.explanation: The chapter ends with hope for the house of Israel. After dispersion, God will gather it again, sanctify itself in the midst of it before the nations and will cause it to dwell in the land given to Jacob. Houses and vineyards symbolize pactual stability, peace and blessing. The security of Israel will contrast with the fate of the peoples who despised it, and all will recognize the LORD as their God.

study.context: The chapter is located in the set of oracles against Tyre and its associated cities. The notes provided treat the text as a historical denunciation against the ruler of Tyre and the city of Sidom, without requiring the reader to abandon this literal sense. Some commentators also note that the language of lamentation has a highly symbolic tone and can echo images of fall and exile used in other biblical texts, but this should not erase the historical sense of confrontation with the king of Tyre and Sidon.
study.theology: Ezekiel 28 teaches that human pride is deeply offensive to God, especially when economic and political power is used to fuel a pretense of self-reliance. The chapter counterposes the appearance of wisdom to moral reality: wealth, prestige, and commercial success do not sanctify anyone. On the contrary, when they come together with arrogance and violence, they become instruments of condemnation. The text also reaffirms that God rules the nations to reveal their holiness and their identity as Lord. His judgment is not only destructive; he also protects his people and restores them. The final promise shows that God's faithfulness to his covenant remains despite the unfaithfulness of the nations and the humiliations suffered by Israel. The security of the restored people does not come from human covenants, but from the sovereign action of God.

scholarViews.insight: The prince of Tyre exalted himself because of his wisdom and wealth; his arrogance led to ruin, and his death as an uncircumcised one indicates a break with the covenant with God.

The lamentation of the king of Tyre shows that, although he was externally admirable, his iniquity destroyed him; the text may also suggest a symbolic echo of the fall of those who rebelled against God.
The expression about the death of the "incircumcised" is understood as temporal and also spiritual judgment; the king of Tyre would not escape the end decreed by God.

questions: In what ways can pride disguise itself in competence, success, or spiritual intelligence in our lives?
What does the text teach about the difference between the appearance of greatness and reality before God?
How can the final promise of restoration sustain faith when God's people suffer opposition and contempt?
study.practice: Examine areas in which success, money, influence or recognition have fueled excessive self-confidence. Confess to God any claim for spiritual independence. Practice gratitude and simplicity, remembering that gifts and opportunities exist to serve, not to exalt the ego. At the same time, strengthen hope in God's faithfulness: he remains able to restore, protect and give security to his people. In situations of injustice or humiliation, rest in the fact that the Lord sees, judges and also brings together those who belong to him.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text and the notes provided allow a clear historical reading of the prince and king of Tyre, and of Sidon, but the language of 28:12-19 is poetic and highly symbolic; therefore, readings that see there an echo of the angelic fall exist in the notes, but are not unanimously required by the text. It is also not possible, based only on the material provided, to identify with absolute certainty the exact historical names behind each title beyond what the commentators suggest.
